title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
prompt:
Given the `root` of a binary tree (not necessarily a search tree) and the values `p` and `q` of two nodes guaranteed to exist in the tree, return the value of their lowest common ancestor (LCA) — the deepest node that has both nodes as descendants (a node is allowed to be a descendant of itself).

The tree is given as a level-order array where `null` marks a missing child (the standard LeetCode serialization). Your function receives this array along with the values `p` and `q`; the starter code includes a helper that builds the tree from the array, so you only need to find and return the LCA's value.

examples.explanation: Nodes 5 and 1 are in different subtrees of the root, so the root itself is their LCA.
Node 4 is a descendant of node 5, so 5 is its own LCA with node 4.

constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [2, 10^5]
p and q both exist in the tree and p != q
hints: Unlike the BST version, you can't use value comparisons to decide direction — you have to search both subtrees.
Recurse into left and right subtrees looking for p or q; a node is a candidate answer if it itself is p or q, or if both subtrees report finding one of the targets.
If a call returns a non-null result from both the left and right recursive calls, the current node is the LCA; if only one side returns non-null, propagate that result upward unchanged.

solution.approach: Recursively search each subtree for p and q. The base case: if the current node is None, or matches p or q, return it directly. Otherwise recurse into left and right children. If both recursive calls return a non-None node, it means p and q were found in different subtrees, so the current node is the LCA. If only one side returns non-None, that result (already resolved deeper down, or one of the targets itself) propagates upward unchanged.
